Roncalli did not stay in the city where Titian died in his later years—Venice—because his career required a move to Rome.  The 16th‑century Italian painter Cristoforo Roncalli (also called *Il Pomarancio*) was born in Pomarance, worked in Siena, and **in about 1578 he “relocated to Rome, where he was commissioned by the Compagnia di Santa Caterina to paint two scenes from the Life of St. Catherine.”** 【8†L55-L60】.  

Rome was by far the most important artistic centre of the time, offering larger commissions, a closer connection to the papacy, and the chance to work with leading artists such as Niccolò Circignani.  The move allowed Roncalli to secure prestigious projects in Rome’s churches and palaces (e.g., the frescoes in Santa Maria di Loreto, the mosaic design for the *Cappella Clementina* in St. Peter’s, and the baptisms of Constantine and St. Simon in San Giovanni in Laterano).  Thus his departure from Venice was driven by the pursuit of greater artistic opportunities and patronage in Rome rather than any personal or political motive.

_**The Bacchanal of the Andrians**_ or _**The Andrians**_ is an oil painting by Titian. It is signed "TICIANUS [F.[aciebat]](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/faciebat "wiktionary:faciebat")" and is dated to 1523–1526.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-prado-1)

# _The Bacchanal of the Andrians_
## History
[edit]
The painting was made by Titian for the Sala dei Baccanali in the [Camerini d'alabastro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camerini_d'alabastro "Camerini d'alabastro") for [Alfonso I d'Este](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_I_d'Este,_Duke_of_Ferrara "Alfonso I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara"), after _The Worship of Venus_ (1518–1519) and _Bacchus and Ariadne_ (1520–1523) and Titian's intervention on _The Feast of the Gods_ by Bellini in 1524–1525 where he retouched the landscape to match the style of the other paintings.
In 1598, control of Ferrara passed to the Papal State and the Este family had to withdraw to Modena. During the transfer, cardinal and papal legate Pietro Aldobrandini appropriated many paintings, among which were _The Bacchanal_ and _The Worship of Venus_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-2) Aldobrandini never exhibited the taken paintings. His theft only became known in 1629 after the paintings had come into the Ludovisi inheritance and then were sold to the Duke of Monterrey in payment of the Principality of Piombino. They were then donated to Philip IV of Spain in 1639.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-3) The first documentation of the paintings in Spain date to the inventories of the Royal Alcázar of Madrid in 1666, 1686, and 1700.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-4)
A Rubens copy of _The Bacchanal_

# _The Bacchanal of the Andrians_
## History
The three canvases of Titian were admired and copied as much in Italy as in Spain by artists like Pieter Paul Rubens, Guido Reni, Nicolas Poussin, and Diego Velázquez, and they contributed to the development of the Baroque style. Rubens' copies of _The Bacchanal_ are housed at the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-prado-1) The Italian artist Domenichino famously wept upon hearing that the masterpieces had left Italy.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-Zuffi-5):70
In 1782, British painter Joshua Reynolds admired _The Bacchanal_, which inspired him to draw a parallel between Titian and the Latin poet Virgil:
> "What was said of Virgil, that he threw even filth about the ground with an air of dignity, may be applied to Titian; whatever he touched, however naturally mean and habitually familiar, by a kind of magic he invested with grandeur and importance."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-6)
The painting is now held at the Museo del Prado in Madrid.

"The stream of wine which is on the island of Andros, and the Andrians who have become drunken from the river, are the subject of this painting. For by act of Dionysus the earth of the Andrians is so charged with wine that it bursts forth and sends up for them a river." From this description in Philostratus' Imagines came the third of Titian's paintings for Alfonso d'Este's camerino. Selecting among the details of the ancient ekphrasis, Titian re-created the image of the peculiarly blessed island and its inhabitants, "the men, crowned with ivy and bryony . . . singing to their wives and children, some dancing on either bank, some reclining." On the hill in the right middle ground "the river [god] lies on a couch of grape-clusters, pouring out its stream." And the Andrians have guests on this occasion: "Dionysus also sails to the revels of Andros and, his ship now moored in the harbor, he leads a mixed throng of Satyrs and Bacchantes and all the Sileni." Deities and mortals, respectively distinguished by their nudity and clothing, mingle and share the benefits of the river.

(b. 1490, Pieve di Cadore, d. 1576, Venezia)
* * *

# Bacchanal of the Andrians by TIZIANO Vecellio
### Bacchanal of the Andrians
1523-24
Oil on canvas, 175 x 193 cm
Museo del Prado, Madrid  
In 1516 Titian made contact with Alfonso I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara for whom he was to work for a decade on pictures destined for the Alabaster Chamber. In this period he painted a series of magnificent paintings of Dionysian themes: the Worship of Venus in the Prado, The Andrians (Bacchanalia), also in the Prado, and Bacchus and Ariadne, in the National Gallery, London. In these paintings Titian combines a richness of colouristic expression with a great formal elegance. These are the elements which characterize this whole so-called "classic" phase of Titian's development and which is dominated by the supreme masterpiece of the Frari Assumption of the Virgin.
The Bacchanal of the Andrians was the last in the series, The subjects are taken from classical descriptions of works of art: here Titian reproduces a picture the writer Philostratus saw in Naples in the second century AD, representing the people of the Greek Island of Andros making merry on the river of wine that Dionysus had created. This splendid opportunity to emulate the past was not lost on Titian, whose brilliant naturalism and marvellous colour declare him the equal of Apelles.
The subject of this painting refers to the arrival of Bacchus on the island of Andros, where his followers await him in varying degrees of inebriation, as they drink from the island's river flowing not with water, but with wine. The god himself is not present, but his ship can be glimpsed in the distance and the Bacchanalian essence is exalted in the flask of wine held unsteadily aloft. The shifting shadows may evoke the checkered moods of intemperance, but there is no moral disapproval and the mood is elegiac and tolerant. The choice of subject may reflect not only the hedonism of the patron but also the agricultural prosperity of the Ferrarese countryside, replete with food and drink.
The man leaning on his elbow in the centre derives from Michelangelo's Battle of Cascina cartoon, while the drunken nymph to the far right is based on a classical statue of Ariadne.

They were then donated to Philip IV of Spain in 1639.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-3) The first documentation of the paintings in Spain date to the inventories of the Royal Alcázar of Madrid in 1666, 1686, and 1700.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-4)

# _The Bacchanal of the Andrians_
## History
The three canvases of Titian were admired and copied as much in Italy as in Spain by artists like Pieter Paul Rubens, Guido Reni, Nicolas Poussin, and Diego Velázquez, and they contributed to the development of the Baroque style. Rubens' copies of _The Bacchanal_ are housed at the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-prado-1) The Italian artist Domenichino famously wept upon hearing that the masterpieces had left Italy.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-Zuffi-5):70
In 1782, British painter Joshua Reynolds admired _The Bacchanal_, which inspired him to draw a parallel between Titian and the Latin poet Virgil:
> "What was said of Virgil, that he threw even filth about the ground with an air of dignity, may be applied to Titian; whatever he touched, however naturally mean and habitually familiar, by a kind of magic he invested with grandeur and importance."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bacchanal_of_the_Andrians#cite_note-6)
The painting is now held at the Museo del Prado in Madrid.

# Bacchanal of the Andrians by TIZIANO Vecellio
### Bacchanal of the Andrians
1523-24
Oil on canvas, 175 x 193 cm
Museo del Prado, Madrid  
In 1516 Titian made contact with Alfonso I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara for whom he was to work for a decade on pictures destined for the Alabaster Chamber. In this period he painted a series of magnificent paintings of Dionysian themes: the Worship of Venus in the Prado, The Andrians (Bacchanalia), also in the Prado, and Bacchus and Ariadne, in the National Gallery, London. In these paintings Titian combines a richness of colouristic expression with a great formal elegance. These are the elements which characterize this whole so-called "classic" phase of Titian's development and which is dominated by the supreme masterpiece of the Frari Assumption of the Virgin.
The Bacchanal of the Andrians was the last in the series, The subjects are taken from classical descriptions of works of art: here Titian reproduces a picture the writer Philostratus saw in Naples in the second century AD, representing the people of the Greek Island of Andros making merry on the river of wine that Dionysus had created. This splendid opportunity to emulate the past was not lost on Titian, whose brilliant naturalism and marvellous colour declare him the equal of Apelles.
The subject of this painting refers to the arrival of Bacchus on the island of Andros, where his followers await him in varying degrees of inebriation, as they drink from the island's river flowing not with water, but with wine. The god himself is not present, but his ship can be glimpsed in the distance and the Bacchanalian essence is exalted in the flask of wine held unsteadily aloft. The shifting shadows may evoke the checkered moods of intemperance, but there is no moral disapproval and the mood is elegiac and tolerant. The choice of subject may reflect not only the hedonism of the patron but also the agricultural prosperity of the Ferrarese countryside, replete with food and drink.
The man leaning on his elbow in the centre derives from Michelangelo's Battle of Cascina cartoon, while the drunken nymph to the far right is based on a classical statue of Ariadne.

"The stream of wine which is on the island of Andros, and the Andrians who have become drunken from the river, are the subject of this painting. For by act of Dionysus the earth of the Andrians is so charged with wine that it bursts forth and sends up for them a river." From this description in Philostratus' Imagines came the third of Titian's paintings for Alfonso d'Este's camerino. Selecting among the details of the ancient ekphrasis, Titian re-created the image of the peculiarly blessed island and its inhabitants, "the men, crowned with ivy and bryony . . . singing to their wives and children, some dancing on either bank, some reclining." On the hill in the right middle ground "the river [god] lies on a couch of grape-clusters, pouring out its stream." And the Andrians have guests on this occasion: "Dionysus also sails to the revels of Andros and, his ship now moored in the harbor, he leads a mixed throng of Satyrs and Bacchantes and all the Sileni." Deities and mortals, respectively distinguished by their nudity and clothing, mingle and share the benefits of the river.

Tiziano Vecellio, known in English as Titian, was born in Pieve di Cadore (then ruled by Venice), probably in 1488/1490. This date is more convincing than that of 1477 justified for a long time by traditional accounts, one being the statement of the clerk of his parish who wrote down in the city’s records that Tiziano died “at the age of one hundred and three years”. Coming from a well-known and important family native from the valleys of Cadore, as a young boy, when he was about 10 to 12 years old, Tiziano together with his brother Francesco were sent to Venice under the tutelage of an uncle to find apprenticeship with a painter. The mosaicist Sebastiano Zuccato, who had a painting school and was probably a family friend, arranged for the brothers to enter the studio of Gentile Bellini. Little is known of Tiziano’s childhood, perhaps captivated by the beauty of Cadore’s mountains that later reappeared frequently in the admirable background landscapes of his paintings. But was precisely Venice, with its opulence, its marbles, its mosaics and lagoon, which enlivened in Tiziano’s eyes and heart that passionate taste for color that made him the painter par excellence.
“Only Tiziano should be credited with the glory of perfect coloring”, commented Lodovico Dolce in 1557, and also did Marco Boschini in 1674: “Actually, Tiziano has been the most excellent of those who have painted, since his brushes always gave light the expressions of life”.

In Venice, painting still relied on the last splendorous works by Vittore Carpaccio, on those by Gentile Bellini, on the expanded spaces and soft colors of Giovanni Bellini‘s chiaroscuro, and on the new way to see the world portrayed by the young Giorgione with his atmospheric, sweet languid tones. From the mosaicist Sebastiano Zuccato “the boy Tiziano was sent to Gentile Bellini, Giovanni’s brother”, and then “… he was told by Gentile that he was not going to be of any use in painting, since he was far away from his master’s style. That is why Tiziano, leaving Gentile, had the opportunity to approach Giovanni Bellini, but not fully liking the way the master painted either, he chose Giorgio da Castelfranco” (Lodovico Dolce).
For Tiziano, Giovanni Bellini represented all the Venetian painting of the 1400’s which was closing with him, while with Giorgione, Tiziano entered the 1500’s art scene more splendid and triumphant. Tiziano Vecellio, as we shall see, had a long life and worked continuously from his early youth to his old age without ever repeating himself, especially in expressions and language, often sketching and abandoning his works to resume them after some months or even years. Tiziano became one of the most versatile of painters in Italy, equally talented with portraits, landscape backgrounds, and mythological and religious subjects. His painting methods and the application and use of color, strongly influenced not only painters of the late Italian Renaissance, but future generations of Western artists. A chronological succession of his paintings is difficult and problematic, and it is not possible in these brief paragraphs to review them all, just as the division of his long life into periods is approximate and, on some occasions, confusing.

On the other hand, from the first years of his collaboration with Giorgione at the _Fondaco dei Tedeschi_ (the state-warehouse for the German merchants in Venice), Tiziano’s work appeared different from that of his teacher. The images he painted already had a more human, earthly and “terrible” beat, and they were situated almost arrogantly in space, in easy-going and confident attitudes, in a new twist of lights that opened up infinite and incredible possibilities of expression to color. Color that will be the great magic by Tiziano at all times during his artistic career and in every genre of painting to which he dedicated his prodigious brush. Portraits, religious paintings, pagan allegories (which he called his “poems”) are frequently intertwined in his prodigious and tireless production. Throughout his life so rich in honors, he remained a painter above all, always aloof from contemporary historical, political and religious events. His spirit perceived neither the struggles of foreign powers to dominate Italy nor the struggle between Reformation and Counter-Reformation, between Christianity and the Muslim world. They were, at best, be the pretext and subject for famous portraits or high-sounding allegories. In the end, Tiziano didn’t feel much attracted by the papal power that emanated from Rome, a city to which he will arrive only until his mature age. And above all, Venice and his environment, his family and the Cadore spoke to his heart forever. His frescoes on the façade of the _Fondaco dei Tedeschi_ are lost, frescoes he executed in the period of his collaboration with Giorgione, around 1508, and that were destroyed in the 1700’s due to the marine salobrity of the lagoon. The first works truly by Tiziano are the **Three Stories of Saint Anthony**, a fresco he painted in the _Scuola del Santo_(“School of the Saint”) in Padua.

View of the _Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua (Italy). The photo shows the entrance wall with two of Titian’s frescoes and the altar wall of the room. The _Scuola del Santo_ in Padua was the place where the brotherhood of St. Anthony met, it is located on the edge of the square in front of the church in which the famous Franciscan saint was buried. Between 1510-1511 Tiziano worked alongside other painters to decorate two walls in the upper Prior’s Room (_Sala Priorale_) with frescoes depicting miracles from the saint’s life. He painted three scenes from the Life of St. Anthony of Padua: The Miracle of the Newborn, The Miracle of the Healed Foot, and The Miracle of the Jealous Husband. These frescoes are the first of Tiziano’s works that can be definitely dated and that still exist in their entirety.
The Miracle of the Newborn Child, fresco, by Tiziano, 1511, 340 x 355 cm (_Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua, Italy). One of Tiziano’s scenes frescoed for the _Scuola del Santo_ depicts The Miracle of the Newborn Child: St. Anthony performed a miracle in which a newly born child spoke in defense of his mother, who had been accused of adultery. The closely observed, very individual faces show Tiziano’s mastery of his art, even at this early stage of his career.
The Miracle of the Healed Foot, fresco, by Tiziano, 1511, 340 x 207 cm (_Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua, Italy). In this scene depicting the Miracle of the Healed Foot, Tiziano shows us St. Anthony reattaching the foot of a young man who had cut it off in an outburst of violent temper because he had hurt his mother with it. Despite the difficulty of working on frescoes, which demanded great speed on the part of the artist, Tiziano succeeded in producing splendid landscapes.

The Miracle of the Jealous Husband, fresco, by Tiziano, 1511, 340 x 185 cm (_Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua, Italy). This scene depicts the Miracle of the Jealous Husband: a jealous husband stabs his wife and then, overcome with remorse, appeals to St. Anthony, who restores her to health. Tiziano shows us here emotional extremes, a singular drama that dominates the entire structure of the painting with artfully composed and interlocked groups of figures. The raised arm of the wife was actually sculpted in relief rather than painted illusionistically.
They can be dated between 1510 and 1512. In these three frescoes depicting the miracles performed by Anthony of Padua, the human figure already triumphs, with the strength of its feeling, alive and attached to the life around it, in a full and continuous conversation. They are clear images and stories open to the viewer, tied to the common thread of a balanced and safe logic. They seem like episodes of everyday life that develop the narrative of the three miracles with the vibrancy of their colors: the newborn who testifies in favor of his mother (**The miracle of the newborn**), the healed foot (**The miracle of the healed foot**) and the injured woman (**The miracle of the jealous husband**). The **Pastoral Concert** (1508-1510, Louvre), perhaps begun by Giorgione but certainly painted by a very young Tiziano, displays a presentiment of a vivid reality that unites man and nature in a happy song of beauty understood in the most ideal and incorruptible sense of classicism. We see now that, from his early twenties, Tiziano Vecellio declared himself a man of the Renaissance, as Raphael and Michelangelo did in their time.

Pastoral Concert, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, 1508-1510, 110 x 138 cm (_Musée du Louvre_, Paris). This work is one of the mysteries of European painting: opinions are divergent concerning both its creator and its theme, in the past it was attributed to Giorgione. The painting has been interpreted as an allegory of Nature, similar to Giorgione’s The Tempest, though its message must be more complex than that. It is believed that the master author consciously unified several themes in this painting, and in consequence the deciphering of symbols required a certain degree of erudition. Modern research has concluded that the composition may represent an allegory of poetry, but some other interpretations are plausible. The female figures in the foreground are probably the Muses of poetry. The standing female pouring water from a glass jar represents the superior tragic poetry, while the seated one holding a flute is the Muse of the less prestigious comedy or pastoral poetry. The well-dressed youth who is playing a lute is the poet of exalted lyricism, while the one without a hat is an ordinary lyricist. The painter based this differentiation on Aristotle’s “_Poetica_“. The scenery shows contrasting environments: while between the slim trees towards the left-center, we see a multi-levelled villa, on the right, within a lush grove, we see a shepherd playing a bagpipe. Yet this contrast appears completely unified. The author achieved harmony between scenery and figures, colors and forms which as a whole provide a close interrelationship between man and nature, poetry and music. The name of the painting was an 18th century attribute, and from there on the Pastoral genre was created based on this painting. Several recognized artists have copied this painting, Édouard Manet conceived his _Le déjeuner sur l’herbe_ after viewing this canvas in the Louvre museum. The poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti wrote a poem titled _A Venetian Pastoral, by Giorgione, in the Louvre_, which was explicitly written inspired in this painting.

In 1512 his fame perhaps began to exceed the confines of the Veneto, and he was invited to Rome by Pietro Bembo. He declined the invitation and preferred to offer his services to the _Serenissima_ Venetian Republic. Then in 1512, from Padua he returns to Venice. The moment is perfect for his arrival. Giorgione died of the plague in 1510, Carpaccio lived isolated in the lucid world of his fantasies, Sebastiano del Piombo was in Rome and Lorenzo Lotto, restless and humble, has left Veneto forever. Only Giovanni Bellini, now old, can contend the palm of victory to Tiziano, who was only 24 years old. In 1513 he was set to paint for the Hall of the Great Council in the Ducal Palace, a large canvas that would be completed many years later, depicting the battle of Cadore, a battle in which his father fought against the Emperor Maximilian. It was going to be a great undertaking that “no man to date has wanted to carry out”, and in return Tiziano asked for the commissions of _La Senseria_, a profitable privilege much coveted by artists in the _Fondaco dei Tedeschi_, which belonged to Giorgione, and for the commissions left unfinished by Giovanni Bellini in the Hall of the Great Council of the Ducal Palace. The artist opened his studio on the Grand Canal in San Samuele and thus began his relationship with the _Serenissima_, which was to last uninterruptedly until his death. The **Great Battle of Cadore** (completed ca. 1538-1539) was destroyed by fire in 1577 and is only known from drawings and some old copies.

The Battle of Cadore, engraving, etching on paper, by Giulio Fontana after an original by Tiziano,1569. The Venetian army powered by local men won a battle against the Holy Roman Emperor in 1508, in a battle that took place in and around the mountain community of Cadore where Tiziano was born. In the 1530’s he was commissioned to paint a scene from this famous victory to be placed inside the Doge’s Palace. For this canvas, Tiziano chose to represent the moment when the Venetian army attacked the enemy and pushed it down into a river. The painting was destroyed by fire in 1577 but we know its composition from an etching made by Giuliano Fontana. Like Michelangelo in his Battle of Cascinaand Leonardo in his Battle of Anghiari have done years before,Tiziano used this scene of violence to depict the creative struggle in his own mind. The bridge represents his eye and the allegory is even more personal by the battle’s location, his own birthplace.Through the bridge, which is both the symbol and shape of Tiziano’s eye, we see a man clinging to a rock rounded like an iris. Another rock by his waist is Titian’s “pupil” partly under water as well. The symbolism has never been seen before because convention assumes that artists illustrate what they are told to. As in similar masterpieces both by Leonardo and Michelangelo we are here witnessing ‘behind’Tiziano’s eyes and mind.

From these early Venetian years are several excellent works in which Tiziano seemed to evoke, with his return to Venice and its lagoon, the spirit and world of his teacher Giorgione, who had recently died. These works are: **St. Mark Enthroned** (ca. 1508-1511) a small altarpiece now in the Church of _Santa Maria della Salute_, the **Portrait of a Lady** (also known as **_La Schiavona_**, 1510-1512, National Gallery in London) and **A Man with a Quilted Sleeve** (known as **Ariosto**, ca. 1510, National Gallery in London). In the first, which was previously in _Santo Spirito in Isola_, the link with the Giorgionesque altarpiece of Castelfranco is evident, “an altarpiece that”, as Vasari says, “many believed was due to the hand of Giorgione”. A visible link between this work and that by Giorgione can be seen in the monumental construction that places Saint Mark high, on his base, perfectly centered between the four Saints in “sacred conversation”. But in the sky there is a wide opening enlarged by the wind that drives the clouds away.

Saint Mark Enthroned with Saints Cosmas and Damian, Roch and Sebastian, oil on panel, by Tiziano, 1508-1511, 230 x 149 cm (Church of _Santa Maria della Salute_,Venice). This altarpiece is a brilliantly colored, luminous work. It is thought to be Tiziano’s first independent commission. This painting was made by a young Tiziano, probably during or shortly after the horrific outbreak of the plague in 1510. It was originally commissioned for the church of _Santo Spirito in Isola_ to celebrate the end of such plague (now it is located in the sacristy of the church of _Santa Maria della Salute_). At the center of the composition, Saint Mark, patron saint of Venice, sits enthroned upon a high pedestal; he holds his gospel in his right hand, leaning it upon his knee. He is framed by two pairs of standing male saints on the pavement below. On the left are Saints Cosmas and Damian, the patron saints of physicians, for they were doctors themselves; on the right appear Saints Roch and Sebastian, the two saints most frequently associated with the plague and particularly invoked in Venice during times of pestilence. It is notable that Saint Mark’s face is dramatically obscured, as are his left arm and shoulder, by the shadow that is cast by the structure to the right; this may represent the plight of Venice during this time of crisis, as well as the city’s hope for salvation. The painting clearly shows the influence of Giovanni Bellini and of Giorgione, who died in 1510.
In **_La_****_Schiavona_** and in **A Man with a Quilted Sleeve** (probably a portrait of a gentleman named Girolamo Barbarigo, a friend of Tiziano who had given him access to ducal favors), the creative energy of Tiziano is already affirmed, unmistakable, in the confident, almost reckless approach to composition, and in the vibrant colors and the play of light.

Portrait of a Lady (also known as ‘_La Schiavona_‘), oil on canvas, by Tiziano, ca. 1510-1512, 119.4 x 96.5 cm (National Gallery, London). Tiziano painted this portrait when he was in his early twenties. The title _La Schiavona_, meaning ‘the Dalmatian woman’, was given to the picture in the 17th century. Dalmatia, on the eastern shores of the Adriatic, was a colony of the Venetian Republic from 1420 to 1797. The identity of the sitter is unknown. She appears remarkably self-possessed and has a commanding gaze unlike any woman in an earlier European portrait at the time. The very strong sense of realism and physical presence of the sitter was also new. The picture is original not only because the portrait is three-quarter length and apparently life-sized (unusually large for a portrait then), but also because it was painted to make an impact from a distance. Portraits of women were unusual in Venice and also uncommon in the work by Tiziano in the early years of the 16th century. Those he did paint, with the exception of anonymous beauties, were the wives of great princes. It seems likely that this work was painted by Tiziano to encourage similar commissions, rather than being a portrait in the traditional sense. The profile bust portrait in relief, inspired by ancient Roman sculpture and cameos, appears to represent the sitter herself but may commemorate a member of her family. If the painting was not a commissioned portrait, it may have been intended to prove the powers of painting over those of sculpture. The letters ’T.V.’ inscribed on the parapet below the woman stand for Tiziano Vecellio. In his handling and treatment of transparent fabrics, such as the veil over the woman’s shoulders and her hairnet, we can see the starting point of Tiziano’s mature style of painting.

The sitter in ****A Man with a Quilted Sleeve**** was thought to be Ariosto, in confirmation of the friendship that probably united the painter and the poet, who in his “Orlando Furioso” says: _“… e Tizian che onora non men Cador, che quei Venezia e Urbino_” (“… and Tiziano who honors Cadore, like those who honor Venice and Urbino”). After Giorgione’s death in 1510, Tiziano’s style slowly developed its own features, including bold and expressive brushwork, one of his landmarks.
A Man with a Quilted Sleeve, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, ca. 1510, 81.2×66.3 cm (National Gallery,London). The identity of the sitter has been the subject of much discussion. This painting may be Tiziano’s earliest portrait. It was long thought to be a portrait of Ariosto, and later a self-portrait. In it, the master shows the personality and “physical assurance” of his sitter with new force and realism. By having the large sleeve project slightly beyond the parapet, Tiziano “subverts” the usual barrier effect, bringing the picture space into “our space” as viewers. The turning pose, with the head slightly atilt and an eyebrow appearing raised, exactly halfway across the composition, adds life and drama.The sleeve is brilliantly painted, and the merging of the shadowed portions of the figure with the grey atmospheric background is one of the most innovative and influential aspects of the painting. The widely spaced letters “T V” appear as though carved into the stone parapet either side of the sleeve, with triangular dots around them. They are usually taken as Tiziano’s initials. Like many other paintings, this particular work was at times attributed to Giorgione, up to well into the 20th century. The pose was borrowed in two self-portraits by Rembrandt, who saw the painting (or a copy) in Amsterdam.

Prior to 1516, are London’s **_Noli me tangere_** (ca. 1514, National Gallery) and Florence’s **Concert** (ca. 1510-1511, _Galleria Palatina_). In the first predominates the wide panorama of nature and, perhaps, it is the first valid example of Tiziano’s inclination for landscape compositions that light up in rich colors among the joyous light of sunsets. It is the first notation by Tiziano of those great landscapes that will open up in his mature works over wide valleys, over the imposing mountains and valleys of Cadore, the landscape of his childhood, the Dolomite mountains Antelao, Pelmo and Marmarole that were deep in his heart and which came to life in the soft atmospheres of his altarpieces, and that also in his allegories, at times, almost became the protagonists.

In that same year of 1516 Giovanni Bellini died and Brother Germano, prior of the convent of _Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari_, commissioned Tiziano with the great altarpiece of the **Assumption****of the Virgin** (1516-1518) to be placed on the altar in the main apse of the temple. The work was inaugurated on March 20, 1518 and was incredibly new and revolutionary for its time. It became the very center of the great choir and of the church itself, and thus the object of prayer and adoration. It is an imposing image by its dizzying mass dynamism and impetuous flash of colors. The image of Mary stands out in the foreground, in a bold foreshortening from bottom to top, illuminated by a pulsating light in the background of the sky and that also illuminates the Eternal and the cloud of his cherubs from above, but that appears appeasing in the Lower part of the painting by soft and deep shadows, with the restless stirring of the Apostles who, due to the energy of their lines and the solidity of their masses, seem to come out of the picture-plane. This work, after some initial dissensions due to the audacity of the new approach, marked the fame of the artist “detached from now on from previous ties with Giorgionism”.

Assumption of the Virgin, oil on panel, by Tiziano, 1516–1518, 690×360 cm (_Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari_,Venice). This was Tiziano’s first major commission for a church in Venice, and brought his work to great public attention. This large altarpiece remains in the original position it was designed for, on the high altar of the _Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari_. It is the largest altarpiece in Venice, with the figures well over life-size. Tiziano painted it _in situ_ in the church. The figures are arranged in three zones, divided by spaces filled only with light. On the ground are the 12 Apostles, tightly packed in a group and in a variety of dramatic poses, most looking up at the unprecedented sight of the Virgin Mary rising to heaven; Saint Peter sits at the center with his hands together in prayer, and Saint John the Evangelist is the younger man in red to the left of him. In the center zone, the Virgin Mary stands on clouds, wrapped in a red robe and blue mantle, also making a gesture of astonishment. Around her, tight groups of angels swirl with the clouds irradiated by light. Above is God the Father, who is about to be handed a crown to be placed on Mary’s head by the angel to the right. For his interpretation of the subject, Tiziano broke with tradition by omitting all landscape elements, although the blue-grey sky above the apostles implies that the scene is set outdoors. The sky contrasts with the golden heavenly light in the upper zones, which recalls the gold background traditional in mosaics such as those still being made inSaint Mark’s Basilica, and the gold ground paintings of the Gothic period representing the heavens. The painting is signed “TITIANUS” on the sarcophagus below the seated figure of St. Peter. This painting is frequently compared to the Transfiguration by Raphael as both compositions have obvious similarities, with an isolated main figure in the air, and below, a crowd of agitated followers who are not fully lit.

In the years from 1516 to 1520 Tiziano worked for Alfonso I d’Este. The account books of the Este Castle tell, in 1516 precisely, of salad, salted meat, oil, chestnuts, oranges, candles, cheese and wine that were delivered each week to the painter, and not of particular works entrusted to him. Although a few years later, around 1518, this assumption was confirmed in a letter from Tiziano to Duke Alfonso himself. Tiziano even added a landscape to Giovanni Bellini’s “Feast of the Gods” and painted the two **Bacchanalia**, currently in the Prado (**The Bacchanal of the Andrians**, 1523-1526, and **The Worship of Venus**, 1518-1519), which, together with the **Triumph of Bacchus and Ariadne** (1522-1523, National Gallery, London) were mythological scenes destined for the small study (_camerino_) of Alfonso I in his castle of Ferrara, paintings that have been many times imitated but never surpassed, even by great masters as Rubens. These paintings are like songs of pagan joy, in which ancient myths seem to be renewed in the sweet softness of the landscape that welcomes and accompanies the movements of the characters, sometimes unbridled, with their natural and serene sensuality, almost purified by the treatment of color that splendidly harmonizes nature with the human figure. The warm ranges of reds, yellows and blues intertwine with the golden green of the forests and soften with the blue of the sky, turning the figures into ancient statuary and true “poems”. _Poesie_ (“Poems”) is what Tiziano called his pagan mythologies, down to the Danaë, the Ledas, the Venuses, and all the goddesses of his later years.

The Worship of Venus, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, 1518–1519, 172×175 cm (_Museo del Prado_,Madrid). In 1516 Tiziano was contacted by Alfonso I d’Este, Duke of Ferrara for whom he was later to work for a decade on a series of mythological paintings destined for his Alabaster Chamber. For this purpose, Tiziano painted a series of magnificent paintings of Dionysian themes: the Worship of Venus (pictured above), The Bachanal of the Andrians and Bacchus and Ariadne (see both below).The first painting in this series is The Worship of Venus, whose subject is Love as the source of fertility and regeneration in nature. Tiziano’s composition is based on a description by the late antique writer Philostratus, in his ‘_Imagines_‘, of a painting of cupids gathering apples in the presence of Venus amid a tree-girt landscape. The painting shows a Roman rite of worship conducted in honor of the goddess Venus that took place each 1 April. Two nymphs, one young and one matronly, are situated to the right of the ceremony, attending to a shrine holding a statue of Venus. The shrine is surrounded by votive tablets. The older woman checks on the decorations with the use of a mirror which she holds high in her extended right hand. The foreground of the canvas is thronged with a swarm of male infants, or _putti_, who distract themselves in activities such as climbing trees, leaping, flying, gathering apples, lying around, fighting, fondling, shooting arrows and pulling each other’s hair. A dam is shown in the middle background, near a sunlit meadow. The far distance is occupied by an open and serene landscape that includes a mountain and blue sky.

Bacchus and Ariadne, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, 1522–1523, 176.5×191 cm (National Gallery,London). This is the second painting made by Tiziano on a cycle on mythological subjects produced for Alfonso I d’Este, Duke of Ferrara, for the _Camerino d’Alabastro_, a private room in his _palazzo_ in Ferrara that was decorated with paintings based on classical texts. In the case of Bacchus and Ariadne, the subject matter was derived from texts by the Roman poets Catullus and Ovid. The painting, considered one of Titian’s greatest works, represents the passage in which Ariadne has been left on the island of Naxos, deserted by her lover Theseus, whose ship sails away to the far left. She is discovered on the shore by the god Bacchus, who’s leading a procession of revelers in a chariot drawn by two cheetahs(these were probably modelled on those in the Duke’s menagerie and were tigers in Ovid’s original text). Bacchus is depicted in mid-air as he leaps out of the chariot to protect Ariadne from these beasts. Bacchus falls in love with Ariadne at first sight, and though she shows initial fear of the god, he ultimately raised her to heaven and turned her into a constellation, represented by the stars above her head (the star constellation _Corona Borealis_ or Northern crown). Tiziano divided the composition diagonally into two triangles, one of blue sky (using the expensive ultramarine pigment) and the other with the group of revelers to the right and predominantly green/brown in color. The King Charles Spaniel dog that barks at the boy satyr in the center foreground is a common motif in Tiziano’s work and was probably a court pet. Towards the left corner, the gold urn inscribed with the artist’s signature (TICIANVS) may also have been familiar to the Duke as one of the antiquities he had in his collection.

Tiziano Vecellio, known in English as Titian, was born in Pieve di Cadore (then ruled by Venice), probably in 1488/1490. This date is more convincing than that of 1477 justified for a long time by traditional accounts, one being the statement of the clerk of his parish who wrote down in the city’s records that Tiziano died “at the age of one hundred and three years”. Coming from a well-known and important family native from the valleys of Cadore, as a young boy, when he was about 10 to 12 years old, Tiziano together with his brother Francesco were sent to Venice under the tutelage of an uncle to find apprenticeship with a painter. The mosaicist Sebastiano Zuccato, who had a painting school and was probably a family friend, arranged for the brothers to enter the studio of Gentile Bellini. Little is known of Tiziano’s childhood, perhaps captivated by the beauty of Cadore’s mountains that later reappeared frequently in the admirable background landscapes of his paintings. But was precisely Venice, with its opulence, its marbles, its mosaics and lagoon, which enlivened in Tiziano’s eyes and heart that passionate taste for color that made him the painter par excellence.
“Only Tiziano should be credited with the glory of perfect coloring”, commented Lodovico Dolce in 1557, and also did Marco Boschini in 1674: “Actually, Tiziano has been the most excellent of those who have painted, since his brushes always gave light the expressions of life”.
texts.1:
In Venice, painting still relied on the last splendorous works by Vittore Carpaccio, on those by Gentile Bellini, on the expanded spaces and soft colors of Giovanni Bellini‘s chiaroscuro, and on the new way to see the world portrayed by the young Giorgione with his atmospheric, sweet languid tones. From the mosaicist Sebastiano Zuccato “the boy Tiziano was sent to Gentile Bellini, Giovanni’s brother”, and then “… he was told by Gentile that he was not going to be of any use in painting, since he was far away from his master’s style. That is why Tiziano, leaving Gentile, had the opportunity to approach Giovanni Bellini, but not fully liking the way the master painted either, he chose Giorgio da Castelfranco” (Lodovico Dolce).
For Tiziano, Giovanni Bellini represented all the Venetian painting of the 1400’s which was closing with him, while with Giorgione, Tiziano entered the 1500’s art scene more splendid and triumphant. Tiziano Vecellio, as we shall see, had a long life and worked continuously from his early youth to his old age without ever repeating himself, especially in expressions and language, often sketching and abandoning his works to resume them after some months or even years. Tiziano became one of the most versatile of painters in Italy, equally talented with portraits, landscape backgrounds, and mythological and religious subjects. His painting methods and the application and use of color, strongly influenced not only painters of the late Italian Renaissance, but future generations of Western artists. A chronological succession of his paintings is difficult and problematic, and it is not possible in these brief paragraphs to review them all, just as the division of his long life into periods is approximate and, on some occasions, confusing.
texts.2: On the other hand, from the first years of his collaboration with Giorgione at the _Fondaco dei Tedeschi_ (the state-warehouse for the German merchants in Venice), Tiziano’s work appeared different from that of his teacher. The images he painted already had a more human, earthly and “terrible” beat, and they were situated almost arrogantly in space, in easy-going and confident attitudes, in a new twist of lights that opened up infinite and incredible possibilities of expression to color. Color that will be the great magic by Tiziano at all times during his artistic career and in every genre of painting to which he dedicated his prodigious brush. Portraits, religious paintings, pagan allegories (which he called his “poems”) are frequently intertwined in his prodigious and tireless production. Throughout his life so rich in honors, he remained a painter above all, always aloof from contemporary historical, political and religious events. His spirit perceived neither the struggles of foreign powers to dominate Italy nor the struggle between Reformation and Counter-Reformation, between Christianity and the Muslim world. They were, at best, be the pretext and subject for famous portraits or high-sounding allegories. In the end, Tiziano didn’t feel much attracted by the papal power that emanated from Rome, a city to which he will arrive only until his mature age. And above all, Venice and his environment, his family and the Cadore spoke to his heart forever. His frescoes on the façade of the _Fondaco dei Tedeschi_ are lost, frescoes he executed in the period of his collaboration with Giorgione, around 1508, and that were destroyed in the 1700’s due to the marine salobrity of the lagoon. The first works truly by Tiziano are the **Three Stories of Saint Anthony**, a fresco he painted in the _Scuola del Santo_(“School of the Saint”) in Padua.
texts.3:
View of the _Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua (Italy). The photo shows the entrance wall with two of Titian’s frescoes and the altar wall of the room. The _Scuola del Santo_ in Padua was the place where the brotherhood of St. Anthony met, it is located on the edge of the square in front of the church in which the famous Franciscan saint was buried. Between 1510-1511 Tiziano worked alongside other painters to decorate two walls in the upper Prior’s Room (_Sala Priorale_) with frescoes depicting miracles from the saint’s life. He painted three scenes from the Life of St. Anthony of Padua: The Miracle of the Newborn, The Miracle of the Healed Foot, and The Miracle of the Jealous Husband. These frescoes are the first of Tiziano’s works that can be definitely dated and that still exist in their entirety.
The Miracle of the Newborn Child, fresco, by Tiziano, 1511, 340 x 355 cm (_Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua, Italy). One of Tiziano’s scenes frescoed for the _Scuola del Santo_ depicts The Miracle of the Newborn Child: St. Anthony performed a miracle in which a newly born child spoke in defense of his mother, who had been accused of adultery. The closely observed, very individual faces show Tiziano’s mastery of his art, even at this early stage of his career.
The Miracle of the Healed Foot, fresco, by Tiziano, 1511, 340 x 207 cm (_Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua, Italy). In this scene depicting the Miracle of the Healed Foot, Tiziano shows us St. Anthony reattaching the foot of a young man who had cut it off in an outburst of violent temper because he had hurt his mother with it. Despite the difficulty of working on frescoes, which demanded great speed on the part of the artist, Tiziano succeeded in producing splendid landscapes.
texts.4:
The Miracle of the Jealous Husband, fresco, by Tiziano, 1511, 340 x 185 cm (_Sala Priorale_, _Scuola del Santo_, Padua, Italy). This scene depicts the Miracle of the Jealous Husband: a jealous husband stabs his wife and then, overcome with remorse, appeals to St. Anthony, who restores her to health. Tiziano shows us here emotional extremes, a singular drama that dominates the entire structure of the painting with artfully composed and interlocked groups of figures. The raised arm of the wife was actually sculpted in relief rather than painted illusionistically.
They can be dated between 1510 and 1512. In these three frescoes depicting the miracles performed by Anthony of Padua, the human figure already triumphs, with the strength of its feeling, alive and attached to the life around it, in a full and continuous conversation. They are clear images and stories open to the viewer, tied to the common thread of a balanced and safe logic. They seem like episodes of everyday life that develop the narrative of the three miracles with the vibrancy of their colors: the newborn who testifies in favor of his mother (**The miracle of the newborn**), the healed foot (**The miracle of the healed foot**) and the injured woman (**The miracle of the jealous husband**). The **Pastoral Concert** (1508-1510, Louvre), perhaps begun by Giorgione but certainly painted by a very young Tiziano, displays a presentiment of a vivid reality that unites man and nature in a happy song of beauty understood in the most ideal and incorruptible sense of classicism. We see now that, from his early twenties, Tiziano Vecellio declared himself a man of the Renaissance, as Raphael and Michelangelo did in their time.
texts.5: Pastoral Concert, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, 1508-1510, 110 x 138 cm (_Musée du Louvre_, Paris). This work is one of the mysteries of European painting: opinions are divergent concerning both its creator and its theme, in the past it was attributed to Giorgione. The painting has been interpreted as an allegory of Nature, similar to Giorgione’s The Tempest, though its message must be more complex than that. It is believed that the master author consciously unified several themes in this painting, and in consequence the deciphering of symbols required a certain degree of erudition. Modern research has concluded that the composition may represent an allegory of poetry, but some other interpretations are plausible. The female figures in the foreground are probably the Muses of poetry. The standing female pouring water from a glass jar represents the superior tragic poetry, while the seated one holding a flute is the Muse of the less prestigious comedy or pastoral poetry. The well-dressed youth who is playing a lute is the poet of exalted lyricism, while the one without a hat is an ordinary lyricist. The painter based this differentiation on Aristotle’s “_Poetica_“. The scenery shows contrasting environments: while between the slim trees towards the left-center, we see a multi-levelled villa, on the right, within a lush grove, we see a shepherd playing a bagpipe. Yet this contrast appears completely unified. The author achieved harmony between scenery and figures, colors and forms which as a whole provide a close interrelationship between man and nature, poetry and music. The name of the painting was an 18th century attribute, and from there on the Pastoral genre was created based on this painting. Several recognized artists have copied this painting, Édouard Manet conceived his _Le déjeuner sur l’herbe_ after viewing this canvas in the Louvre museum. The poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti wrote a poem titled _A Venetian Pastoral, by Giorgione, in the Louvre_, which was explicitly written inspired in this painting.
texts.6: In 1512 his fame perhaps began to exceed the confines of the Veneto, and he was invited to Rome by Pietro Bembo. He declined the invitation and preferred to offer his services to the _Serenissima_ Venetian Republic. Then in 1512, from Padua he returns to Venice. The moment is perfect for his arrival. Giorgione died of the plague in 1510, Carpaccio lived isolated in the lucid world of his fantasies, Sebastiano del Piombo was in Rome and Lorenzo Lotto, restless and humble, has left Veneto forever. Only Giovanni Bellini, now old, can contend the palm of victory to Tiziano, who was only 24 years old. In 1513 he was set to paint for the Hall of the Great Council in the Ducal Palace, a large canvas that would be completed many years later, depicting the battle of Cadore, a battle in which his father fought against the Emperor Maximilian. It was going to be a great undertaking that “no man to date has wanted to carry out”, and in return Tiziano asked for the commissions of _La Senseria_, a profitable privilege much coveted by artists in the _Fondaco dei Tedeschi_, which belonged to Giorgione, and for the commissions left unfinished by Giovanni Bellini in the Hall of the Great Council of the Ducal Palace. The artist opened his studio on the Grand Canal in San Samuele and thus began his relationship with the _Serenissima_, which was to last uninterruptedly until his death. The **Great Battle of Cadore** (completed ca. 1538-1539) was destroyed by fire in 1577 and is only known from drawings and some old copies.
texts.7: The Battle of Cadore, engraving, etching on paper, by Giulio Fontana after an original by Tiziano,1569. The Venetian army powered by local men won a battle against the Holy Roman Emperor in 1508, in a battle that took place in and around the mountain community of Cadore where Tiziano was born. In the 1530’s he was commissioned to paint a scene from this famous victory to be placed inside the Doge’s Palace. For this canvas, Tiziano chose to represent the moment when the Venetian army attacked the enemy and pushed it down into a river. The painting was destroyed by fire in 1577 but we know its composition from an etching made by Giuliano Fontana. Like Michelangelo in his Battle of Cascinaand Leonardo in his Battle of Anghiari have done years before,Tiziano used this scene of violence to depict the creative struggle in his own mind. The bridge represents his eye and the allegory is even more personal by the battle’s location, his own birthplace.Through the bridge, which is both the symbol and shape of Tiziano’s eye, we see a man clinging to a rock rounded like an iris. Another rock by his waist is Titian’s “pupil” partly under water as well. The symbolism has never been seen before because convention assumes that artists illustrate what they are told to. As in similar masterpieces both by Leonardo and Michelangelo we are here witnessing ‘behind’Tiziano’s eyes and mind.
texts.8: From these early Venetian years are several excellent works in which Tiziano seemed to evoke, with his return to Venice and its lagoon, the spirit and world of his teacher Giorgione, who had recently died. These works are: **St. Mark Enthroned** (ca. 1508-1511) a small altarpiece now in the Church of _Santa Maria della Salute_, the **Portrait of a Lady** (also known as **_La Schiavona_**, 1510-1512, National Gallery in London) and **A Man with a Quilted Sleeve** (known as **Ariosto**, ca. 1510, National Gallery in London). In the first, which was previously in _Santo Spirito in Isola_, the link with the Giorgionesque altarpiece of Castelfranco is evident, “an altarpiece that”, as Vasari says, “many believed was due to the hand of Giorgione”. A visible link between this work and that by Giorgione can be seen in the monumental construction that places Saint Mark high, on his base, perfectly centered between the four Saints in “sacred conversation”. But in the sky there is a wide opening enlarged by the wind that drives the clouds away.
texts.9:
Saint Mark Enthroned with Saints Cosmas and Damian, Roch and Sebastian, oil on panel, by Tiziano, 1508-1511, 230 x 149 cm (Church of _Santa Maria della Salute_,Venice). This altarpiece is a brilliantly colored, luminous work. It is thought to be Tiziano’s first independent commission. This painting was made by a young Tiziano, probably during or shortly after the horrific outbreak of the plague in 1510. It was originally commissioned for the church of _Santo Spirito in Isola_ to celebrate the end of such plague (now it is located in the sacristy of the church of _Santa Maria della Salute_). At the center of the composition, Saint Mark, patron saint of Venice, sits enthroned upon a high pedestal; he holds his gospel in his right hand, leaning it upon his knee. He is framed by two pairs of standing male saints on the pavement below. On the left are Saints Cosmas and Damian, the patron saints of physicians, for they were doctors themselves; on the right appear Saints Roch and Sebastian, the two saints most frequently associated with the plague and particularly invoked in Venice during times of pestilence. It is notable that Saint Mark’s face is dramatically obscured, as are his left arm and shoulder, by the shadow that is cast by the structure to the right; this may represent the plight of Venice during this time of crisis, as well as the city’s hope for salvation. The painting clearly shows the influence of Giovanni Bellini and of Giorgione, who died in 1510.
In **_La_****_Schiavona_** and in **A Man with a Quilted Sleeve** (probably a portrait of a gentleman named Girolamo Barbarigo, a friend of Tiziano who had given him access to ducal favors), the creative energy of Tiziano is already affirmed, unmistakable, in the confident, almost reckless approach to composition, and in the vibrant colors and the play of light.
texts.10: Portrait of a Lady (also known as ‘_La Schiavona_‘), oil on canvas, by Tiziano, ca. 1510-1512, 119.4 x 96.5 cm (National Gallery, London). Tiziano painted this portrait when he was in his early twenties. The title _La Schiavona_, meaning ‘the Dalmatian woman’, was given to the picture in the 17th century. Dalmatia, on the eastern shores of the Adriatic, was a colony of the Venetian Republic from 1420 to 1797. The identity of the sitter is unknown. She appears remarkably self-possessed and has a commanding gaze unlike any woman in an earlier European portrait at the time. The very strong sense of realism and physical presence of the sitter was also new. The picture is original not only because the portrait is three-quarter length and apparently life-sized (unusually large for a portrait then), but also because it was painted to make an impact from a distance. Portraits of women were unusual in Venice and also uncommon in the work by Tiziano in the early years of the 16th century. Those he did paint, with the exception of anonymous beauties, were the wives of great princes. It seems likely that this work was painted by Tiziano to encourage similar commissions, rather than being a portrait in the traditional sense. The profile bust portrait in relief, inspired by ancient Roman sculpture and cameos, appears to represent the sitter herself but may commemorate a member of her family. If the painting was not a commissioned portrait, it may have been intended to prove the powers of painting over those of sculpture. The letters ’T.V.’ inscribed on the parapet below the woman stand for Tiziano Vecellio. In his handling and treatment of transparent fabrics, such as the veil over the woman’s shoulders and her hairnet, we can see the starting point of Tiziano’s mature style of painting.
texts.11:
The sitter in ****A Man with a Quilted Sleeve**** was thought to be Ariosto, in confirmation of the friendship that probably united the painter and the poet, who in his “Orlando Furioso” says: _“… e Tizian che onora non men Cador, che quei Venezia e Urbino_” (“… and Tiziano who honors Cadore, like those who honor Venice and Urbino”). After Giorgione’s death in 1510, Tiziano’s style slowly developed its own features, including bold and expressive brushwork, one of his landmarks.
A Man with a Quilted Sleeve, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, ca. 1510, 81.2×66.3 cm (National Gallery,London). The identity of the sitter has been the subject of much discussion. This painting may be Tiziano’s earliest portrait. It was long thought to be a portrait of Ariosto, and later a self-portrait. In it, the master shows the personality and “physical assurance” of his sitter with new force and realism. By having the large sleeve project slightly beyond the parapet, Tiziano “subverts” the usual barrier effect, bringing the picture space into “our space” as viewers. The turning pose, with the head slightly atilt and an eyebrow appearing raised, exactly halfway across the composition, adds life and drama.The sleeve is brilliantly painted, and the merging of the shadowed portions of the figure with the grey atmospheric background is one of the most innovative and influential aspects of the painting. The widely spaced letters “T V” appear as though carved into the stone parapet either side of the sleeve, with triangular dots around them. They are usually taken as Tiziano’s initials. Like many other paintings, this particular work was at times attributed to Giorgione, up to well into the 20th century. The pose was borrowed in two self-portraits by Rembrandt, who saw the painting (or a copy) in Amsterdam.
texts.12: Prior to 1516, are London’s **_Noli me tangere_** (ca. 1514, National Gallery) and Florence’s **Concert** (ca. 1510-1511, _Galleria Palatina_). In the first predominates the wide panorama of nature and, perhaps, it is the first valid example of Tiziano’s inclination for landscape compositions that light up in rich colors among the joyous light of sunsets. It is the first notation by Tiziano of those great landscapes that will open up in his mature works over wide valleys, over the imposing mountains and valleys of Cadore, the landscape of his childhood, the Dolomite mountains Antelao, Pelmo and Marmarole that were deep in his heart and which came to life in the soft atmospheres of his altarpieces, and that also in his allegories, at times, almost became the protagonists.
texts.22: In that same year of 1516 Giovanni Bellini died and Brother Germano, prior of the convent of _Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari_, commissioned Tiziano with the great altarpiece of the **Assumption****of the Virgin** (1516-1518) to be placed on the altar in the main apse of the temple. The work was inaugurated on March 20, 1518 and was incredibly new and revolutionary for its time. It became the very center of the great choir and of the church itself, and thus the object of prayer and adoration. It is an imposing image by its dizzying mass dynamism and impetuous flash of colors. The image of Mary stands out in the foreground, in a bold foreshortening from bottom to top, illuminated by a pulsating light in the background of the sky and that also illuminates the Eternal and the cloud of his cherubs from above, but that appears appeasing in the Lower part of the painting by soft and deep shadows, with the restless stirring of the Apostles who, due to the energy of their lines and the solidity of their masses, seem to come out of the picture-plane. This work, after some initial dissensions due to the audacity of the new approach, marked the fame of the artist “detached from now on from previous ties with Giorgionism”.
texts.23: Assumption of the Virgin, oil on panel, by Tiziano, 1516–1518, 690×360 cm (_Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari_,Venice). This was Tiziano’s first major commission for a church in Venice, and brought his work to great public attention. This large altarpiece remains in the original position it was designed for, on the high altar of the _Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari_. It is the largest altarpiece in Venice, with the figures well over life-size. Tiziano painted it _in situ_ in the church. The figures are arranged in three zones, divided by spaces filled only with light. On the ground are the 12 Apostles, tightly packed in a group and in a variety of dramatic poses, most looking up at the unprecedented sight of the Virgin Mary rising to heaven; Saint Peter sits at the center with his hands together in prayer, and Saint John the Evangelist is the younger man in red to the left of him. In the center zone, the Virgin Mary stands on clouds, wrapped in a red robe and blue mantle, also making a gesture of astonishment. Around her, tight groups of angels swirl with the clouds irradiated by light. Above is God the Father, who is about to be handed a crown to be placed on Mary’s head by the angel to the right. For his interpretation of the subject, Tiziano broke with tradition by omitting all landscape elements, although the blue-grey sky above the apostles implies that the scene is set outdoors. The sky contrasts with the golden heavenly light in the upper zones, which recalls the gold background traditional in mosaics such as those still being made inSaint Mark’s Basilica, and the gold ground paintings of the Gothic period representing the heavens. The painting is signed “TITIANUS” on the sarcophagus below the seated figure of St. Peter. This painting is frequently compared to the Transfiguration by Raphael as both compositions have obvious similarities, with an isolated main figure in the air, and below, a crowd of agitated followers who are not fully lit.
texts.24: In the years from 1516 to 1520 Tiziano worked for Alfonso I d’Este. The account books of the Este Castle tell, in 1516 precisely, of salad, salted meat, oil, chestnuts, oranges, candles, cheese and wine that were delivered each week to the painter, and not of particular works entrusted to him. Although a few years later, around 1518, this assumption was confirmed in a letter from Tiziano to Duke Alfonso himself. Tiziano even added a landscape to Giovanni Bellini’s “Feast of the Gods” and painted the two **Bacchanalia**, currently in the Prado (**The Bacchanal of the Andrians**, 1523-1526, and **The Worship of Venus**, 1518-1519), which, together with the **Triumph of Bacchus and Ariadne** (1522-1523, National Gallery, London) were mythological scenes destined for the small study (_camerino_) of Alfonso I in his castle of Ferrara, paintings that have been many times imitated but never surpassed, even by great masters as Rubens. These paintings are like songs of pagan joy, in which ancient myths seem to be renewed in the sweet softness of the landscape that welcomes and accompanies the movements of the characters, sometimes unbridled, with their natural and serene sensuality, almost purified by the treatment of color that splendidly harmonizes nature with the human figure. The warm ranges of reds, yellows and blues intertwine with the golden green of the forests and soften with the blue of the sky, turning the figures into ancient statuary and true “poems”. _Poesie_ (“Poems”) is what Tiziano called his pagan mythologies, down to the Danaë, the Ledas, the Venuses, and all the goddesses of his later years.
texts.25: The Worship of Venus, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, 1518–1519, 172×175 cm (_Museo del Prado_,Madrid). In 1516 Tiziano was contacted by Alfonso I d’Este, Duke of Ferrara for whom he was later to work for a decade on a series of mythological paintings destined for his Alabaster Chamber. For this purpose, Tiziano painted a series of magnificent paintings of Dionysian themes: the Worship of Venus (pictured above), The Bachanal of the Andrians and Bacchus and Ariadne (see both below).The first painting in this series is The Worship of Venus, whose subject is Love as the source of fertility and regeneration in nature. Tiziano’s composition is based on a description by the late antique writer Philostratus, in his ‘_Imagines_‘, of a painting of cupids gathering apples in the presence of Venus amid a tree-girt landscape. The painting shows a Roman rite of worship conducted in honor of the goddess Venus that took place each 1 April. Two nymphs, one young and one matronly, are situated to the right of the ceremony, attending to a shrine holding a statue of Venus. The shrine is surrounded by votive tablets. The older woman checks on the decorations with the use of a mirror which she holds high in her extended right hand. The foreground of the canvas is thronged with a swarm of male infants, or _putti_, who distract themselves in activities such as climbing trees, leaping, flying, gathering apples, lying around, fighting, fondling, shooting arrows and pulling each other’s hair. A dam is shown in the middle background, near a sunlit meadow. The far distance is occupied by an open and serene landscape that includes a mountain and blue sky.
texts.26: Bacchus and Ariadne, oil on canvas, by Tiziano, 1522–1523, 176.5×191 cm (National Gallery,London). This is the second painting made by Tiziano on a cycle on mythological subjects produced for Alfonso I d’Este, Duke of Ferrara, for the _Camerino d’Alabastro_, a private room in his _palazzo_ in Ferrara that was decorated with paintings based on classical texts. In the case of Bacchus and Ariadne, the subject matter was derived from texts by the Roman poets Catullus and Ovid. The painting, considered one of Titian’s greatest works, represents the passage in which Ariadne has been left on the island of Naxos, deserted by her lover Theseus, whose ship sails away to the far left. She is discovered on the shore by the god Bacchus, who’s leading a procession of revelers in a chariot drawn by two cheetahs(these were probably modelled on those in the Duke’s menagerie and were tigers in Ovid’s original text). Bacchus is depicted in mid-air as he leaps out of the chariot to protect Ariadne from these beasts. Bacchus falls in love with Ariadne at first sight, and though she shows initial fear of the god, he ultimately raised her to heaven and turned her into a constellation, represented by the stars above her head (the star constellation _Corona Borealis_ or Northern crown). Tiziano divided the composition diagonally into two triangles, one of blue sky (using the expensive ultramarine pigment) and the other with the group of revelers to the right and predominantly green/brown in color. The King Charles Spaniel dog that barks at the boy satyr in the center foreground is a common motif in Tiziano’s work and was probably a court pet. Towards the left corner, the gold urn inscribed with the artist’s signature (TICIANVS) may also have been familiar to the Duke as one of the antiquities he had in his collection.

**Cristoforo Roncalli** (8 September 1552–14 May 1626) was an Italian mannerist painter. He was one of the three painters known as _Pomarancio_ or _Il Pomarancio_.
Roncalli was born in Pomarance, a small town near Volterra, to a well-to-do merchant family. He first studied in Florence. By 1575 he had moved to Siena, where Ippolito Agostini commissioned him to paint an altarpiece for the cathedral, a _Virgin and Child with St. Anthony and St. Agatha_ (1576; Siena, [Museo dell'Opera del Duomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_dell'Opera_del_Duomo_(Siena) "Museo dell'Opera del Duomo (Siena)")), and to fresco a ceiling in Agostini’s palace (now Palazzo Bindi Sergardi) with allegories from Ovid’s _Metamorphoses_. Giulio Mancini (1621) said that Roncalli was associated with Prospero Antichi and suggested the importance of the art of Domenico Beccafumi for the cathedral altarpiece.

Around 1578, Roncalli relocated to Rome, where he was commissioned by the Compagnia di Santa Caterina to paint two scenes from the _Life of St. Catherine_ (Siena, Santuario di Santa Caterina), pictures still indebted to Florentine and Sienese Mannerism. He established his career in Rome with frescoes in the oratory of the Crocefisso at San Marcello al Corso, where he had first collaborated with Niccolò Circignani on part of a cycle of frescoes showing the _Discovery and Exaltation of the True Cross_. In 1585–6, he frescoed the Mattei and Valli chapels in Santa Maria in Ara Coeli with scenes from the Passion of Christ and scenes from the _Life of St._ Paul, works that were deeply influenced by a wide variety of Mannerist artists.
In 1588, he became a member of the Accademia di San Luca. He also won the protection and friendship of the Crescentii and through them was introduced to the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri, for whom he painted scenes from the _Life of St. Filippo Neri_ (1596–9; Rome, Santa Maria in Vallicella, chapel of San Filippo Neri). These are distinguished by a new realism and more dramatic contrasts of light and shade.
_Pope Sylvester baptizes Constantine_, Saint John Lateran, Rome
In 1597 Pope Clement VIII, in connection with the Holy Year, embarked on two major public commissions, for the decoration of [St. Peter's Basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter's_Basilica "St. Peter's Basilica") and Saint John Lateran. He chose painters trained in the classical traditions of Florentine art, and Roncalli was commissioned to paint the _Baptism of Constantine_ and _St. Simon_ in the transept of San Giovanni in Laterano and to prepare designs for the mosaic decoration in the Clementine Chapel, St Peter’s, where he collaborated with Giuseppe Cesari.

In a perceptive analysis, Mancini described the four dominant schools of early 17th-century painting in Rome: those of Caravaggio and of the Carracci, late Mannerism (represented by the Cavaliere d’Arpino) and a style epitomized by Roncalli, which might be termed eclectic. He cites as examples of two distinct stylistic veins in Roncalli’s art the altarpiece _St. Domitilla with St. Nereus and St. Achilleus_ (1596; Rome, Santi Nereo e Achilleo) and the frescoes in Santa Maria in Ara Coeli: he describes one as ‘more powerful’, the other as ‘pleasing and graceful’.
In the papal commissions, Roncalli moved away from his early Mannerism towards a more classical and monumental style. His mature art drew again on his early experience of Florentine painting and on a deepening knowledge of the work of Raphael and of Michelangelo. Yet at the same time, he absorbed new influences, from Francesco Salviati and Correggio, while retaining an awareness of the art of Federico Zuccari.
In 1605, Roncalli won a commission for a major cycle of frescoes in the new sacristy of the basilica of Santa Maria at Loreto. Bands of gilt stucco divide the ceiling geometrically and frame elegant scenes from the _Life of the Virgin_, which glow with iridescent colour. In 1606, Roncalli interrupted this work and accompanied Marchese Giustiniani, Marchese Vincenzo on a tour of Germany, Flanders, France and England. In 1609, having finished the frescoes in the sacristy, he was commissioned to fresco the cupola of Santa Maria, Loreto. There is a bozzetto for the vast fresco of the Coronation of the Virgin (Loreto, Basilica della Santa Casa, Bib.) and preparatory drawings (many at Loreto, Basilica della Santa Casa, Bib.).

Many highly accomplished, sculptural drawings in both red and black chalk reveal the meticulous care with which Roncalli prepared his paintings. They include compositional studies, figure drawings, sketches from life, drawings after the Antique and detailed studies of parts of figures. Roncalli was named a Knight of the Supreme Order of Christ in 1607. He died in Rome in 1626. His pupils included Alessandro Casolano, and his son Ilario Casolano.

Cristoforo RONCALLI
* * *
Pomarance 1552 - Rome 1626
Cristoforo RONCALLI
Pomarance 1552 - Rome 1626
Biography
Little is known of Cristoforo Roncalli’s artistic training. Known as Il Pomarancio after his birthplace of Pomarance, he is first documented working in Siena between 1576 and 1579. During this period he painted an altarpiece for the Duomo and collaborated on the decoration of a family palazzo, and also received a commission for an altarpiece intended for the church of SS. Apostoli in Florence. Roncalli then settled in Rome, where he is recorded by 1582, and was active there for the remainder of his career. He was associated with a circle of artists active in the city that included his compatriot Niccolò Circignani (confusingly also known as Il Pomarancio) as well as Cavaliere d’Arpino, Cesare Nebbia and Paris Nogari. Roncalli received numerous public and private commissions, and was admitted to the Accademia di San Luca in 1588.

He earned a reputation as an ecclesiastic mural painter of the first rank, gaining the patronage of such Roman families as the Crescenzi, Mattei and Giustiniani, and working in the churches of Santa Maria in Aracoeli, San Giovanni Decollato, Santa Maria in Vallicella and San Silvestro in Capite in Rome. Between 1599 and 1604 he supervised the decoration of the Cappella Clementina in St. Peter’s for Pope Clement VIII, and also worked for the Pope on the decoration of the transept of San Giovanni in Laterano. Around 1607 Roncalli was named a cavaliere di christo by Pope Paul V, shortly after receiving the most significant commission of his career; the fresco decoration of the sacristy and cupola of the Basilica of the Santa Casa at Loreto, on which he worked between 1605 and 1615. On his return to Rome, Roncalli spent the last decade of his career working on more modest commissions.
An exceptional draughtsman, Roncalli worked for the most part in both black and red chalk, switching easily between them for both compositional and figural studies, although using the former slightly more in the 1580’s and 1590’s. (While a number of pen drawings by the artist are known, after the 1580’s he seems to have worked almost exclusively in chalk.) His earliest datable drawings – studies for works of the late 1570’s, as well as copies after Raphael - already show a mastery of form and line and a sophistication that would be characteristic of the artist’s drawings throughout his career. The largest extant group of drawings by Roncalli is today in the Uffizi.
